landing.welcome_title: Welcome to the MVPF Analysis Dashboard

info_tile.heading: What is MVPF?
info_tile.description: The Marginal Value of Public Funds (MVPF) is a metric that measures the social welfare benefit of a policy per dollar of government spending. It represents how much value beneficiaries receive relative to what the policy costs. [link to MIT page]
info_tile.formula: Most MVPF work looks at policies where the person subject to the policy is also the main beneficiary, such as cash transfers. Detention is different. Jail is imposed on detainees but is justified as benefiting the general public. That is why this tool tracks both Detainee effects and broader Society effects when calculating the MVPF of detention.
info_tile.application_label: Our application of MVPF to Cook County Jail
info_tile.application: In most MVPF work, In most MVPF work, people plug in causal estimates for how behavior changes at the intensive margin (for example, working a bit more or less when a benefit changes). For Cook County Jail, we do not have credible intensive-margin estimates for detention, and the policy questions we are interested in are about the extensive margin and the scale of the jail itself: who is detained at all, for how long, and what level of funding or even continued operation is justified. It uses the full annual costs of operating the jail and the full set of impacts on people who are detained to summarize those tradeoffs in an MVPF-style framework. This CCJ calculator is built to help you see how assumptions about extensive-margin harms and benefits feed into both the numerator and the denominator, using 2018 jail spending as the benchmark.  For a fuller discussion of this choice and its limits, see the longer explanation [link to MVPF Explained].

scenario_selector.label: Select Scenario to calculate the MVPF:

scenarios.description:
The scenarios below offer three different set-ups for how to value the effects of detention on detainees. They differ only in how detainee harm is measured between two options, and whether spillover harms to the detainee’s community are included as well. 
 
Note: There are nearly infinite reasonable normative stances one could take about how to scale the harm of detention to detainees, especially in the absence of a clean experiment. The scenarios in this dashboard do not claim to identify a single “correct” stance. We do suggest a baseline scenario as a useful starting point, but it is only one choice among many reasonable alternatives. Instead, the dashboard provides a structured way to translate different views about detainee harm into concrete MVPF calculations so that policy and value disagreements can be discussed using the same underlying quantities.
scenarios.label: Select Scenario:

baseline.title: Baseline Valuation
baseline.description: In this scenario, detainee harm is valued using the Relative Harm Valuation (RHV) scale. RHV yields a relatively large negative value per day in custody based on an indirect survey of the general population. We do not add any spillover harms to the detainee’s community, on the view that some of those broader harms may already be reflected in RHV. This combination leans on components that are well supported in the literature and keeps extra assumptions to a minimum. It is the default scenario in the dashboard and our recommended starting point for interpretation.

most_conservative.title: Lower-Bound Anchor / Smallest Valuation
most_conservative.description: In this scenario, detainee harm is valued using the smaller Willingness to Pay for Freedom (WTP) scale rather than the larger Relative Harm Valuation (RHV) scale. WTP is based on direct survey responses from people who have experienced jail, producing a much smaller per-day harm estimate than RHV (roughly 300x smaller). Because this scale assigns far less harm to detention, the numerator becomes less negative and the MVPF moves closer to zero. This anchor represents the most detention-favorable valuation of harm in the dashboard.

least_conservative.title: Upper-Bound Anchor / Largest Valuation
least_conservative.value: Uses RHV plus added community spillover harms
least_conservative.description: In this scenario, detainee harm is valued using the same RHV scale as in the baseline anchor, and we add an extra term to capture spillover harms to the detainee’s community that are not already captured by the individual-level value. This additional component makes the total harm assigned to detention larger in magnitude. As a result, the numerator becomes more negative and the MVPF for detention moves further below zero. Among the scenarios, this anchor represents the least detention-favorable valuation of harm.

applying_to_detention.heading: Applying MVPF to detention in Cook County Jail
applying_to_detention.paragraph1: Most MVPF work looks at policies where the person subject to the policy is also the main beneficiary, such as cash transfers. Detention is different. Jail is imposed on detainees but is justified as benefiting the general public. That is why this tool tracks both Detainee effects and broader Society effects when calculating the MVPF of detention.
applying_to_detention.paragraph2: In most MVPF work, people plug in causal estimates for how behavior changes at the intensive margin (for example, working a bit more or less when a benefit changes). For Cook County Jail, we do not have credible intensive-margin estimates for detention, and the policy questions we are interested in are about the extensive margin and the scale of the jail itself: who is detained at all, for how long, and what level of funding or even continued operation is justified. It uses the full annual costs of operating the jail and the full set of impacts on people who are detained to summarize those tradeoffs in an MVPF-style framework. This CCJ calculator is built to help you see how assumptions about extensive-margin harms and benefits feed into both the numerator and the denominator, using 2018 jail spending as the benchmark.
applying_to_detention.paragraph3: To further understand the assumptions behind this approach, we provide a detailed breakdown of each scenario, the parameters, and how they may reflect the broader implications of detention policy. The scenarios and parameter are designed to explore different perspectives on the tradeoffs between public costs and the various social, individual, and government-related harms and benefits associated with detention. Each scenario allows users to adjust key components, such as the detainee value approach, and the parameters allow users to change the multipliers applied to these components, helping to assess the sensitivity of the MVPF to these assumptions. By reviewing the full explanations below, users can better understand the rationale behind the assumptions and how small changes in these variables can lead to different policy recommendations. This will give you a comprehensive view of the complexities and trade-offs inherent in making decisions about the scale and impact of pretrial detention.

purpose.title: Purpose
purpose.description: This dashboard helps policymakers and researchers understand the tradeoffs involved in pretrial detention by quantifying both costs and benefits in a common framework.

methodology.title: Methodology
methodology.description: The MVPF calculation combines three main components to provide a comprehensive view of detention's impact:
methodology.component1: Detainee Values: Quantifying the harm imposed on individuals through detention
methodology.component2: Society Values: Measuring external impacts on public safety and community wellbeing
methodology.component3: Government Costs: Calculating the full fiscal burden of detention operations

data_sources.title: Data Sources
data_sources.description: This analysis relies on empirical evidence from Cook County Jail operations (2018), academic research on detention impacts, and validated cost estimates from government budgets and policy studies.

felony_rate.title: Felony Rate
felony_rate.description: The proportion of detainees charged with at least one felony offense. This parameter affects the severity classification of cases and influences both societal benefits and detainee harm valuations. Higher felony rates typically correlate with longer sentences and greater incapacitation effects.

detainee_population.title: Detainee Population
detainee_population.description: The number of individuals detained at Cook County Jail over the course of a year. This baseline population figure is multiplied by the population multiplier to determine the total detention scale. Changes in this parameter directly affect all cost and benefit calculations proportionally.

length_of_stay.title: Length of Stay
length_of_stay.description: The average number of days individuals are detained in Cook County Jail before resolution of their case. This parameter affects both the per-person harm experienced by detainees and the operational costs borne by the government. Longer stays increase both harms and costs proportionally.

crime_effect.title: Crime Effect
crime_effect.description: The multiplier applied to crime-related impacts of detention on public safety. This parameter reflects assumptions about detention's incapacitation effect (preventing crimes while incarcerated) versus potential criminogenic effects (increased criminal behavior post-release). A value of 0 assumes no net crime impact, positive values assume crime reduction, and negative values assume detention increases future criminal behavior.

baseline.title: Baseline Scenario
baseline.description: Focuses on individual harm to detainees plus potential criminogenic effects of detention. This scenario uses empirically-derived estimates for the willingness-to-pay to avoid detention and includes both direct individual harms and potential increases in future criminal behavior. It represents a middle-ground perspective that acknowledges both the personal costs of incarceration and concerns about criminogenic effects.

most_conservative.title: Conservative Scenario
most_conservative.description: Uses smaller survey-based estimates to value detainee harm, producing less negative MVPF values. This scenario relies on revealed preference studies that provide lower-bound estimates of the harm from detention, excluding broader spillover effects on families and communities. It represents a minimal harm valuation approach that focuses only on direct, measurable impacts on detained individuals.

least_conservative.title: Least Conservative Scenario
least_conservative.description: Includes broad social harms to communities and families, plus criminogenic effects of detention. This scenario incorporates spillover costs to families, neighborhoods, and social networks, alongside individual-level harms. It also accounts for potential increases in criminal behavior following detention. This approach captures the full range of social costs that extend beyond the individual detainee.

detainee_values.title: Detainee Values
detainee_values.description: Detainee Values capture the total harm detention imposes on people who are jailed. We measure this using a willingness-to-pay lens, estimating how much a person would trade to avoid being detained. This reflects short-term harms, disruptions to work and family life, and long-term effects on health, income, and stability.

harm_valuation.button_text: Willingness to Pay derived from Relative Harm Valuation
harm_valuation.explanation: The baseline detainee component, which measures harm by comparing each day in custody to crime-victimization cost benchmarks such as robbery or aggravated assault. This produces a larger per-day harm value than detainee self-reported WTP (~$4,000/day), and scales with whatever length of stay (non-linearly), population, or charge mix the user chooses. Because it reflects broader social harm rather than ability-to-pay limits, it is used as the default. Source: crime-harm equivalence estimates from Stevenson & Mayson (2022).

wtp_freedom.explanation: An alternative detainee valuation based on stated willingness-to-pay (WTP) per day to avoid jail, drawn from surveys of people facing detention. Valued at $11/day in 2018 dollars. This approach reflects detainees' own monetary tradeoffs and can be scaled using any assumed length of stay or detainee population. It typically produces much smaller harm estimates than the baseline Relative Harm Valuation, which makes the overall MVPF less negative and is therefore a more conservative choice. Source: detainee WTP evidence summarized in Stevenson & Mayson (2022).

society_values.title: Society Values
society_values.description: Society Values measure how detention affects external factors like public safety, victimization risk, and community wellbeing. These values summarize the effects felt by people outside the jail and convert those effects into a common dollar scale for comparison.

crime_prevention.explanation: This component captures any crime-prevention benefit from incapacitation during detention. In the baseline model, this is set to zero in line with empirical evidence suggesting minimal net crime reduction from pretrial detention. Users can adjust this assumption in alternative scenarios.

court_appearance.explanation: Included as a baseline society component because court appearance is a central justification for pretrial detention. This component places a dollar value on avoiding failures to appear (FTA) by combining administrative costs of warrant issuance and possible rearrest with an assumed FTA probability. Source: Fishbane, Ouss & Shah (2020) and Cook County court data.

community_spillovers.explanation: This component captures broader community effects of detention, including impacts on families, neighborhoods, and local economies. Effects include lost wages, disrupted caregiving, and reduced community stability. These spillovers extend the costs of detention beyond the individual detainee.

government_cost.title: Government Cost
government_cost.description: Government Cost reflects all public spending required to run the detention system. This includes daily operations, staffing, healthcare, facilities, court processing, and administrative overhead. It represents the fiscal cost taxpayers bear to support the current level of detention.

operational.explanation: The baseline government cost component, representing the full operating budgets for the Cook County Department of Corrections and Cermak Health Services. These expenses include staffing, food, medical care, housing, and other daily operations, and they can be allocated over any assumed detainee count or length of stay. Since these costs reflect actual fiscal outlays, they form the default denominator of the MVPF. Source: Cook County FY2018 Appropriation Budget.

crime_increase.button_text: Costs associated with Crime Effect: Increase
crime_increase.explanation: Government costs that arise if detention leads to increased crime post-release (criminogenic effect). This includes additional law enforcement, court processing, victim services, and potential future incarceration costs. Evidence suggests detention can increase recidivism for some populations.

crime_decrease.button_text: Costs associated with Crime Effect: Decrease
crime_decrease.explanation: Government savings that occur if detention prevents crimes through incapacitation or deterrence. This includes avoided law enforcement costs, reduced court processing, and lower victim compensation. The magnitude depends on assumptions about detention's crime-prevention effectiveness.

overview_intro.title: Understanding MVPF for Cook County Jail
overview_intro.content: A comprehensive analysis of the marginal value of pre-trial detainment and its implications for public policy.
overview_intro.paragraph1: This dashboard lets you explore how different assumptions change the Marginal Value of Public Funds (MVPF) for pretrial detention in Cook County Jail. The MVPF compares the total harms and benefits created by detention to the public cost of operating the jail. You can adjust several inputs that determine the number of people detained, the composition of cases, and the avergae length of stay. These inputs reshape the numerator and denominator of the MVPF and let you test how sensitive the results are to policy or system changes.
overview_intro.paragraph2:
Each scenario shows an MVPF for pretrial detention that compares harms and benefits to the public cost of running Cook County Jail in 2018. In every scenario, the numerator is built from two types of components: 
 • harms to detainees, valued in dollars per day in custody 
 • effects on society, such as changes in court appearance or crime outcomes
overview_intro.paragraph3: The denominator is always the 2018 operating cost of the jail, scaled by the population and length of stay choices you set above, plus any costs or savings associated with crime outcomes.
overview_intro.paragraph4: The scenarios below offer three different normative stances on how to value detention. They differ only in how detainee harm is measured and whether spillover harms to the detainee's community are included. By default, the crime effect parameter is set to zero in every scenario. If you turn on a nonzero crime effect, it will change both the numerator (through assumed social costs or benefits of crime) and the denominator (through changes in government spending on policing, courts, and incarceration). Use these scenarios and parameters to see how alternative value judgments and crime assumptions shift the MVPF and what that implies about the social return of pretrial detention under different assumptions.

mvpf_purpose.title: How the MVPF for Cook County Jail was calculated?
mvpf_purpose.content:
This section will explain the purpose and methodology of the MVPF calculation, including how the baseline values are derived and what they represent in the context of Cook County Jail operations. 
  The metric is calculated by dividing the willingness to pay for a policy by its net government cost. A higher MVPF indicates that beneficiaries value the policy more relative to its cost, making it a more efficient use of public resources.

scenario_intro_p1: The three scenarios differ only in how we value harm to detainees (a larger Relative Harm Valuation scale versus a smaller survey-based "Willingness to Pay for Freedom") and whether we add an extra negative term for spillover harms to the detainee’s community. In all scenarios, the crime effect components are set to zero by default; they only change if you adjust that parameter elsewhere in the dashboard.
